- When sentiment is strongly negative (e.g., < -0.4) over recent days, model tends to overcorrect upward — reduce forecast peak by 5–10%.
- After a sharp price spike (forecast > 70), model often overshoots and fails to correct — cap forecast at +5% above peak or adjust downward by 2–3 points if sentiment turns neutral or negative.
- If sentiment is consistently positive (e.g., > 0.3) and price is trending up, model may overestimate momentum — reduce forecast by 2–5% in the next 5–7 days.
- Model underestimates true volatility when sentiment is mixed or neutral — increase forecast variance by 1–2 points in early horizon (e.g., 1–3 days ahead).
- Mean reversion bias: if forecast is > 75% above 30-day moving average, reduce by 3–5% unless sentiment strongly supports continuation.
- Horizon-specific: 30-day forecasts often overestimate short-term volatility — reduce forecast by 1–3% for days 1–7, especially if sentiment is negative.
- If sentiment history shows repeated “reversal” patterns (e.g., +0.3 → -0.4 → +0.2), model tends to lag — adjust forecast 1–2 days ahead to match sentiment shift.
